title: The physician
hookLine: court physician in Cairo, he advised moderation in everything

lines: CAIRO BY DAY, PATIENTS BY NIGHT.
cards: A courtyard full of people, waiting. Some are Jews, some are not. Some are officials, some are ordinary people.
They're all waiting for one tired man to ride home. Maimonides describes the scene himself, in a letter to Samuel ibn Tibbon, the man translating his work.

He goes up to Cairo early in the day to attend the ruler's household, and comes back to find his house surrounded by patients. He barely eats before he starts seeing them, and he keeps going into the night.

teach.b: The physician. In Hebrew, rofe. First, the job.

The man who wrote a code of all Jewish law and a philosophical guide also earned his living by medicine, serving at the court and treating ordinary people at home. Scholar and doctor, the same person on the same day.
His medical writings keep returning to an idea we've met in his ethics: moderation. Not too much food, not too little. Exercise, but don't exhaust yourself.

teach.h: ONE MEASURE FOR BODY AND MIND.
teach.b: And he watches the mind as well as the body: worry, grief and anger, he warns, take a toll on health, and a settled, cheerful spirit helps a person heal. Third, the link.
His law code gives a doctor's advice about meals and sleep. His medical advice turns to the temper of the mind. The same measure runs through both.
For him, medicine and ethics are one way of thinking, applied twice. Fourth, the healer behind the healer.

teach.h: I AM THE LORD THAT HEALETH THEE.
teach.b: The Torah has God say, "for I am the LORD that healeth thee."
A doctor who believes that doesn't stop practicing medicine. Maimonides worked, prescribed and wrote. Caring for the body and trusting God were not rivals for him.
The tired man in the courtyard does both at once, patient by patient, until the lamps are lit.

how: Jewish tradition honors medicine as a calling, and Jewish law expects a sick person to seek a doctor's care; some Jews read Maimonides' medical advice alongside his laws of character.

o: Maimonides' daily work as a doctor, giving moderate advice
the court official who judged the sultan's household
a rabbi who heals by prayer alone, without medicine

p: received his letter about his day

s: Maimonides was a scholar only, not a working doctor
he earned his living by medicine, at court and with patients at home.
his medical advice and his ethics both point to moderation
not too much, not too little: in food, sleep, exercise and temper.
he paid attention only to the body, not the mind
he warned that worry, grief and anger harm health.

games.q: you're Maimonides. you've spent the day at court in Cairo. you ride home, exhausted, and find your courtyard full of people waiting. what do you do?
o: send them all home until tomorrow.
eat a little, then see patients into the night.
games.why: in his letter, he describes eating briefly and then treating patients, Jews and non-Jews, high and low, into the night.

practice: If you can, stand and walk slowly around the room, not fast, not for a step count, at a middle pace, feeling your heels land and your breath match your steps.
If you can't walk right now, walk in your mind along a short route you know, step by step. Either way, aim for not too much and not too little.

wordCard.voice: The physician. Rofe in Hebrew: Maimonides earned his living as a doctor, and his medicine and his ethics give the same advice. Moderation. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a physician or healer, from the same root as the verb in "the LORD that healeth thee."

carryVoice: Your line: moderation. Not too much, not too little, for body and mind alike. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Letter of Maimonides to Samuel ibn Tibbon
Maimonides, medical writings (e.g. Regimen of Health)
